Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (centres de santé rurale, CSRs) in Côte d'Ivoire predominantly record patient data using paper-based registers and forms at the point of service. Data is manually aggregated into summary reports and transmitted monthly/quarterly to district or regional levels, where it is entered into the national DHIS2 health management information system (HMIS). No evidence indicates routine use of electronic health records (EHR), electronic medical records (EMR), or digital point-of-care entry in most rural clinics; paper remains the default method despite national digital infrastructure like DHIS2 rollout (nationwide since ~2019). Digital systems are limited to isolated pilots or disease-specific programs, such as SIGDEP for HIV patient management (233 sites, electronic but not general care) and recent donor-supported trackers (e.g., cervical cancer screening). The 2021+ PHISICC project redesigns paper tools for better usability in rural Côte d'Ivoire facilities, confirming paper's ongoing dominance and overload on health workers. Key barriers include unreliable electricity/internet in rural areas, limited devices/training, and prioritization of aggregate national reporting over point-of-service digitalisation. Recent plans (2025) aim to connect 1,000 clinics to high-speed internet for telemedicine/digitized records, signaling ambition but current gap. National policy focuses on DHIS2/eLMIS for HMIS/logistics, but rural PoS reality lags: paper collection followed by higher-level transcription, fitting score 2 (predominantly paper with some digital pilots/aggregate tools).

revision_notes: Original row recorded Value Code 1 (Entirely paper) despite the Comments text itself arguing for score 2 - an internal inconsistency. Fetched cited sources (PHISICC protocol, MEASURE Evaluation) confirm paper remains the default at rural clinics. Fresh searches found: a 2024 JMIR survey of DHIS2/MAGPI/SORMAS users confirming that data collection for the two most widely used tools (DHIS2, MAGPI) 'still resorts to paper forms', while SORMAS is fully electronic but confined to a small pilot (2 regions, including rural Gbêkê); and the mHealth.ci platform, launched January 2025 by the Ministry of Health with UNICEF/Ticanalyse support, which equips community and frontline health workers in the largely rural Poro health region (five districts, around 60 health facilities) with smartphones for digital data capture (household registration, antenatal/postnatal follow-up, vaccination), syncing to DHIS2. This is a genuine, documented facility-level digital pilot reaching rural facilities, so the row is recalculated to code 2 (Mostly paper - some digital), aligning the Value Code with the evidence and the original Comments text. Not promoted further as digital capture remains a minority pilot, not the norm.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (centres de santé rurale) in Côte d'Ivoire predominantly rely on paper-based registers for patient data capture, with monthly/quarterly aggregation into the national DHIS2 health information system (SIGSANTE) at district level. However, isolated digital pilots now reach some rural facilities: the mHealth.ci platform, launched in January 2025 by the Ministry of Health with UNICEF support, equips community and frontline health workers in the largely rural Poro health region (five districts, around 60 health facilities) with smartphones for digital data capture on household registration, antenatal/postnatal follow-up and vaccination, syncing directly with DHIS2. The SORMAS disease surveillance system is similarly piloted on a fully electronic basis in a small number of districts, including rural Gbêkê. These remain isolated projects rather than the norm: a 2024 national survey confirms that the two most widely used surveillance tools, MAGPI and DHIS2, still depend on paper forms for data collection at facility level. Overall, paper remains the default recording method in most rural clinics, with genuine but limited pockets of digital capture.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: No specific evidence found of digital recording at rural police stations or gendarmerie brigades in Côte d'Ivoire. Standard francophone practice of handwritten procès-verbaux (police reports) persists, as indicated by models and procedures. Central initiatives exist: CTIP/BTIP for police data processing in Abidjan (Ministry of Interior), WAPIS regional system (INTERPOL), and justice digitalisation (e-justice.ci). US State Dept reports describe arrests/detentions at stations but no digital mention (State.gov 2023). Rural facilities likely paper-based, with possible later central entry (score 1 per rules).

revision_notes: Fetched cited sources; the Ministry of Interior page confirms a November 2024 training workshop for the Centre/Bureau de Traitement des Informations Policières (CTIP/BTIP), and the WAPIS/state department sources are consistent with the original assessment. A fresh search of a 2025 government 'bilan' review found further digitalisation activity (video surveillance covering the 12 police prefectures, interconnection of 105 SIPAO/WAPIS judicial-investigative sites, new stations at Didiévi, Ferkessédougou and Daloa equipped with computer hardware), but all of this concentrates on Abidjan-centred information processing units or general IT equipment in newly built stations, not on digital capture of case records at rural facilities themselves. No evidence found of digital recording of procès-verbaux or custody records at rural stations/gendarmerie posts. Score 1 (Entirely paper) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural police stations and gendarmerie brigades in Côte d'Ivoire continue to record cases, custody and other operational data by hand, using the standard francophone procès-verbal system. Central digitalisation initiatives exist - the Centre/Bureau de Traitement des Informations Policières (CTIP/BTIP), the regional WAPIS/SIPAO information-sharing programme (105 interconnected judicial and investigative sites), and urban video-surveillance (VPU) covering the 12 police prefectures - but these concentrate on Abidjan and other major urban centres and on centralised information processing rather than facility-level data capture. Newly built stations in towns such as Didiévi, Ferkessédougou and Daloa have been equipped with computer hardware, but no evidence indicates that day-to-day recording of incidents and detentions at rural facilities has moved from paper. Data collected on paper is transmitted to central units for later digital processing rather than captured digitally at source.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Côte d'Ivoire predominantly record attendance, enrollment, grades, and admin data on paper. Data flows from schools to regional DRENs then ministry DTSI, often via physical questionnaires causing delays and errors. Digital EMIS/SIGE centralizes aggregates but relies on higher-level entry, not school-level digital recording. SIGE piloted in select regions (Bouaké, San Pedro - mixed urban/rural) and secondary schools; primary extension ongoing but rural coverage limited by infrastructure (62% primary schools lack electricity, 2% have multimedia per SNDECI 2024-28). No evidence of digital at rural facility level; score 2 for pilots/aggregate digital.

revision_notes: The Ministry of Education source (education.gouv.ci/Activite/details/372) could not be fetched (403 error) but the Development Gateway and SNDECI 2024-2028 strategy document were verified directly and corroborate the original account. A fresh search confirms the Système d'Information et de Gestion de l'Éducation (SIGE) was officially launched in July 2025 but currently covers only 24 secondary schools in the Abidjan, Bouaké and San-Pedro regions; SNDECI 2024-2028 states school-management software has been used since 1995 but only by secondary institutions, that extension of digital pupil registration (Fichier National des Élèves) to primary level is 'in progress' (not complete), and that 62% of primary schools lack electricity while only 2% have multimedia equipment. No evidence found of digital data capture at rural primary-school level; the original Comments text argued for score 2 but this is not supported once higher-level digitisation (excluded by the variable's scope) is set aside. The recorded Value Code of 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Côte d'Ivoire continue to record attendance, enrolment, grades and administrative information on paper. Data is transmitted from schools to regional education directorates (DRENs) and then to the ministry's DTSI, typically via physical questionnaires, which the ministry's own strategy document notes causes delays, data-entry errors and administrative burden. The new Système d'Information et de Gestion de l'Éducation (SIGE), officially launched in July 2025 with US/MCC funding, currently covers only 24 secondary schools in the Abidjan, Bouaké and San-Pedro regions; digital school-management software has likewise been used since 1995 but only by secondary institutions. Extension of digital pupil registration (the Fichier National des Élèves) to the primary level remains a work in progress, and the national digitalisation strategy (SNDECI 2024-2028) reports that 62% of primary schools lack electricity and only 2% have multimedia equipment. No evidence indicates routine digital data capture at rural primary-school level; digitalisation, where it exists, occurs through higher-level aggregation rather than at the facility.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Côte d'Ivoire predominantly use paper-based recording for births and vital events, with manual registration at local civil status centers (Bureau de l'État Civil). Birth registration coverage is lower in rural areas (60% in 2016) compared to urban (90%), indicating accessibility issues. A national digital system (Cityweb software by ONECI) is being rolled out, currently in 105 of 860 centers across 5 regions as of early 2024, with plans for 80% by end-2024, enabling digital entry, real-time updates, and no manual transmission. Cityweb Côte d'Ivoire uses fully electronic transmission from local to central levels and outsources data hosting, but lacks dedicated IT staff and details on rural point-of-service digital use. This represents isolated digital pilots/projects amid paper default; no evidence majority rural facilities routinely digital at point of care. Key barriers: rural infrastructure, training, electricity. National ambition (RNPP, e-services) outpaces rural reality, where paper persists for most facilities.

revision_notes: The original score of 2 rested on Cityweb rollout figures current to February 2024 (105 of 860 centres). Both cited sources were fetched and confirmed. Fresh searches show rapid subsequent expansion: 302 of 690 centres by July 2024, and in March 2026 the ONECI director general publicly stated that 98% of civil registry centres nationwide are now computerised and connected to Cityweb. This is a single, self-reported figure delivered in a promotional context (announcement of a birth-registration partnership with the Saint'Egidio community) rather than an independently audited statistic, and it does not break down rural versus urban coverage separately, so it should not be treated as conclusive proof of 'Entirely digital' (the top of this variable's scale). It does, however, indicate that digital capture at the point of registration is now widespread rather than an isolated pilot, supporting a recalculation to 'Mostly digital - some paper' (3) rather than confirming 'Mostly paper - some digital' (2). Given the reliance on one non-independent source for the headline figure, and the strength of the claim, this row is flagged for human review rather than asserted outright, and a promotion to the scale maximum (4, Entirely digital) is not made.
revised_comments: Civil registry offices in Côte d'Ivoire, including those in rural areas, are in the advanced stages of a national digitalisation programme built around the Cityweb software developed with Semlex. Deployment expanded rapidly from 105 of 860 centres (five regions) in February 2024 to 302 of 690 centres by July 2024, and by March 2026 the National Office of Civil Status and Identification (ONECI) reported that 98% of civil status centres nationwide were computerised and connected to Cityweb, enabling electronic recording and near real-time transmission of births, deaths and marriages in place of manual transmission between levels. Historic gaps remain a backdrop to this rollout: birth registration coverage stood at around 60% in rural areas against 90% in urban areas as of 2016, and rural centres have historically faced weaker infrastructure, staffing and connectivity than urban ones. Given the scale and pace of the reported rollout, most registry offices - including in rural areas - now appear to capture civil status data digitally at the point of registration, though a smaller share is likely to still depend on manual back-up processes.
